packages.label: נֶפֶשׁ יְתֵרָה וַהֲסְתַּלְּקוּת הַצַּדִּיק
packages.label_en: The Extra Soul and the Departure of the Tzaddik
packages.reason: The entire teaching rests on a single structural bechina: the grief of the Chavrayya upon Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's impending departure IS a bechina of Shabbat-departure grief — specifically, the grief over losing the Nefesh Yeteirah (extra Shabbat soul) at Motzaei Shabbat. The Talmud (Beitzah 16) derives from 'שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ' (Exodus 31:17) that 'כֵּיוָן שֶׁשָּׁבַת וַי אָבְדָה נֶפֶשׁ' — when Shabbat rests/ceases, 'vay' (woe) — the soul departs. The Rebbe's teaching draws the structural equivalence: the Chavrayya's relationship with Rabbi Shimon parallels Israel's relationship with the Nefesh Yeteirah on Shabbat. Both involve an elevated spiritual state of great pleasure and delight (תַּעֲנוּג / שַׁעֲשׁוּעִים) given through a sacred channel (Shabbat / the Tzaddik), and both produce intense anticipatory grief (גַּעֲגּוּעִים / צַעַר הַהִסְתַּלְּקוּת) upon the perception that this elevated state will end. The polarity is 'neutral' rather than 'good' or 'evil' because the teaching is a structural observation — it identifies a universal phenomenology of elevated spiritual experience and the longing it generates, not a prescription for or against anything. The Tzaddik himself (Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai), the Nefesh Yeteirah, Shabbat, and the quality of spiritual delight (תַּעֲנוּג) all belong to the domain of holiness, but the teaching's argument is structural/descriptive rather than normative/prescriptive. No evil mirror is present in this Torah — it is a short, purely structural analogy without any opposing force or negative polarity.
